Guru Angad

Stories of the Sikh Gurus

Guru Angad

Nanak's Own Limb

In everyday English — the whole story of the second Guru

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story was made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting among family at home — with the smell of the langar and the dust of the wrestling ground in the air.

The yellow boxes are the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little when you read them — Nanak's calm, Lehna's humble, Mata Khivi's loving.

(The purple cues) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader, not the listener.

At the end of every part, the green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listener speak. In this story, those questions matter as much as the story.

There are two kinds of things in this book — Guru Angad's own bani, written in the Guru Granth Sahib, and the stories of the Janamsakhis, told in the sangat for centuries. Where a story comes from the Janamsakhis, the book says so plainly — 'the tradition tells us'. Where the words are Angad's own, the book names them.

This book's main story comes from Angad's bani and the Janamsakhis. The full list of sources is at the end of the book.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Guru Angad — the heart of this story. First Bhai Lehna, then Guru Nanak's successor. The second Guru of the Sikhs.

Bhai Lehna — Angad's first name. Born at Matte di Sarai, a devotee of the Goddess, and later Nanak's most obedient disciple.

Guru Nanak — the first Guru, whose light passed to Angad. In this book he looks as he did in the first book — white beard, white robe, staff in hand, rosary around his neck.

Mata Khivi — Lehna's wife. The soul of the langar at Khadur Sahib — the smell of her cooking travelled far and wide.

Pheru Mal — Lehna's father, a trader of Matte di Sarai.

Mata Daya Kaur (Sabhrai) — Lehna's mother.

Datu and Dasu — Angad's two sons.

Bibi Amro and Bibi Anokhi — Angad's two daughters. It was Bibi Amro's singing that brought Bhai Amardas to Khadur.

Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das — Nanak's two sons. The elder, Sri Chand, later founded the Udasi order of ascetics.

Bhai Jodha — Nanak's disciple, whose words first sent Lehna to Nanak.

Bhai Amardas — the humblest servant of Khadur, who went on to become the third Guru.

Mata Sulakhni — Nanak's wife, who lived at Kartarpur.

1 · Birth — Matte di Sarai · · BIRTH — MATTE DI SARAI

In Ferozepur district there was a small village — Matte di Sarai. It is still called by that name today, in the area of Sri Muktsar Sahib. There, on 31 March 1504, a child was born whose name was Lehna.

The child's father, Pheru Mal, was a trader of the village — he dealt in grain and cloth. His mother, Daya Kaur — whom people also called Sabhrai — kept the home. The house had food, honour, everything.

Lehna was quiet and obedient from childhood. Whatever he was told, he did — without question, without argument. The people of the village said this child carried the words of his elders on his head, as one carries something precious.

When Lehna was fifteen, he married Mata Khivi — a girl from Khadur, who was to become a great name in this story. Then came four children — two sons, Datu and Dasu, and two daughters, Amro and Anokhi.

Lehna's home, his farming, everything was running well. But Lehna's heart reached further than the four walls of his home — he was steeped in devotion to the Goddess, and every year he went on a journey that changed his life.

The date and place of birth

According to the Sikh records, Lehna was born on Baisakh vadi 1, Samvat 1561 — 31 March 1504 at Matte di Sarai (Ferozepur district, near Sri Muktsar Sahib today). This is the date found in most sources — including the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism — and it is the one used in this book.

The marriage to Mata Khivi

Lehna married Mata Khivi in about 1519, when he was fifteen. Khivi was from the village of Khadur — and Khadur was to become the seat of Angad's Guruship.

Pause and think — Lehna obeyed his elders from childhood — without argument. Is obeying a weakness — or the greatest strength? And should every order be obeyed, or are there orders that must be questioned?

2 · The Devotee of the Goddess · · THE DEVOTEE OF THE GODDESS

In Lehna's home there was devotion to the Goddess. His mother and his family were devotees of Devi Durga — and every year, during Navratri, Lehna went on a long journey — into the Kangra hills, to the temple of Jwalamukhi.

At Jwalamukhi the flame of the Goddess burns without oil and without a wick — tongues of fire rising from the rocks of the mountain. People came from far and wide — on foot, weeks of walking, hungry and thirsty, only for a glimpse of the Goddess. Lehna went every year, and every year he took more people from his village with him.

On the way, Lehna served everyone — he carried the old people's bundles, gave water to the weary, and arranged food for all at night. People said — to walk with Lehna is itself a kind of devotion.

But one year, on the way itself, something happened that changed the direction of Lehna's whole journey.

The Jwalamukhi pilgrimage — the tradition's story

Lehna's devotion to the Goddess and his yearly pilgrimage to Jwalamukhi are the Janamsakhis' and Gurbilas's story — the tradition's telling, not a document of history. The tradition of the flame burning at Jwalamukhi (today in Kangra district, Himachal Pradesh) without oil or wick is still honoured there today.

Pause and think — Every year Lehna walked for weeks to see the Goddess. Is there a journey in your life — a place, a task — for which you could labour for weeks?

3 · The Meeting with Nanak · · THE MEETING WITH NANAK

The tradition says that one year, on the way to Jwalamukhi, Lehna's party stopped on the road. There they met a man — Bhai Jodha, a disciple of Nanak. Jodha sang Nanak's bani — and Lehna kept listening.

Jodha said — the Goddess whose glimpse you are climbing the mountain for lives within you. And there is a man — Nanak — at Kartarpur, who sings this very thing.

Lehna asked — (softly) who is Nanak?

Jodha said — he is the one of whom people say — na koi Hindu, na koi Musalman. Go and meet him once.

Lehna let the party go on ahead — and turned himself towards Kartarpur. The road was long, but his feet did not stop.

At Kartarpur Lehna saw a village, fields, a langar, and in the middle an old man — white beard, white robe, staff in hand — driving a plough. That was Nanak.

Lehna bowed before him. Nanak looked at him and said — come, Lehna. You had set out to see the Goddess — but God has called you here.

The tradition says that on that very day Lehna gave up the Jwalamukhi pilgrimage — and stayed with Nanak. The man who had set out to see the Goddess had found the Guru.

The year of the meeting — not certain

The sources do not agree on the year Lehna met Nanak — the traditional reckoning places it in about 1532, some seven years before Nanak's death. Some sources also say around 1530. This book says 'about 1532' in the main story, and records both reckonings here in the note.

Bhai Jodha — the tradition's story

Meeting Bhai Jodha on the road and turning towards Kartarpur on his word is the Janamsakhi's story. Jodha's name is found in the tradition as a disciple of Nanak.

Pause and think — Lehna had set out to see the Goddess — and found the Guru instead. Has it ever happened to you that you set out for one destination, and on the way found another, better one?

4 · The Tests · · THE TESTS

At Kartarpur Nanak had many disciples. But Nanak was asking a question — after me, who? And he was finding the answer by testing them.

The tradition says that one day it was raining. Nanak said to Lehna — Lehna, lift this heavy bundle and follow me. The bundle was of grass, soaked, heavy — and the road was full of mud. Lehna lifted the bundle and walked on — without a single word.

Another day, Nanak's vessel fell into the mud. Nanak said — Lehna, fetch the vessel. Lehna stepped into the mud, took out the vessel, washed it, and placed it in Nanak's hands — as if handing over something precious.

And there was one test harder than all the rest. The tradition says that one day a corpse lay by the roadside — covered with a sheet. Nanak said — whoever is a true disciple, let him eat this corpse. Everyone stepped back. Only Lehna stepped forward. He lifted the sheet — and saw that in place of the corpse, Nanak himself was lying there. Nanak rose and smiled.

There were many such tests — rising at midnight to serve, washing Nanak's clothes, doing the work without being told. Every time, it was Lehna who stood true. The sangat saw — there was no show in Lehna's obedience; it was his habit, his nature.

The stories of the tests — the Janamsakhis' stories

The bundle, the vessel fallen in the mud, and the corpse test are all Janamsakhi stories. Their point is that Nanak tied succession not to birth but to service and obedience. The corpse test also appeared in the first book (§13) — there too it was told as the tradition's story.

Pause and think — In every test Lehna never asked 'why?' — he simply did it. Is obeying itself the greatest test? And is there ever a time when asking 'why?' is the right thing?

5 · Angad — My Own Limb · · ANGAD — MY OWN LIMB

The years passed. Nanak was nearing seventy. In Kartarpur the sangat's question grew deeper — after Nanak, who?

Nanak had two sons — Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das. Sri Chand had become an Udasi ascetic — leaving home and family for the forests and the places of pilgrimage. Lakhmi Das's heart was not in the Guru's seat either.

At last, in 1539, Nanak called Lehna to him. The sangat gathered. Nanak placed his hand on Lehna's head and said —

From today your name is Angad — my own limb, a part of my own body.

The sangat saw — the Guru changed, but the light stayed the same. As one lamp lights another — the flame stays the same, the lamp changes.

Nanak passed his light — his jot — to Angad. And a few days later, on 22 September 1539, Nanak passed away at Kartarpur itself. The sangat wept — but Angad stood there, calm, as if Nanak were still within him.

Angad — what the name means

The name 'Angad' comes from 'ang' — a limb of the body, one's own part. Nanak said Angad was not separate from him — the same light, the same jot. This also appeared in the first book (§13).

When was the name changed?

The tradition says Lehna's name was changed to 'Angad' in 1539, at the moment the Guruship was passed on. In some stories the name 'Angad' is also used earlier — but the main tradition is that the naming and the succession happened in the same hour.

Pause and think — Nanak said — Angad is my own limb. Can a Guru and a disciple truly become one? And in your life, who is there whom you could call your own limb?

6 · Gurmukhi — Giving the Letters Their Form · · GURMUKHI — GIVING THE LETTERS THEIR FORM

After Nanak, Angad's greatest work was to save the bani. Nanak's bani lived in people's hearts, in songs — but it was not written in a book. If the bani was not written down, it would be lost in a single generation.

In Punjab in those days many kinds of writing were in use — traders wrote their accounts in the Landa and Mahajani scripts, and pandits wrote in Devanagari and Persian. But the common person had no writing of his own — none that could hold his speech, his bani, exactly as it was.

Angad took up that work — giving those letters a settled form. He improved the letters, bound them into an order, and began teaching them to children. At Khadur he himself sat children down and taught them the letters — one letter at a time, one word at a time.

And then he began to have Nanak's bani written down in those very letters. The tradition says Angad gathered Nanak's bani together and had it written down for the first time in one place — so that the generations to come could read it as Nanak had sung it.

Today the script in which the Guru Granth Sahib is written, in which Punjabi is written — its name is Gurmukhi — the script of the Guru's mouth. And the one who gave this script its form was Guru Angad.

Gurmukhi — what Angad did, and did not do

It would not be right to say Angad made the letters out of nothing. Letter forms already existed in Punjab's mercantile Landa and Mahajani scripts, and similar letters were written in those days. What Angad did was this — he improved the letters, gave them a settled form, taught them to children, and had Nanak's bani written in them. Modern scholars (such as W. H. McLeod) say the same — Angad's role was to give form and spread the script, not to invent it from nothing. The main story in this book says the same.

Having Nanak's bani written down

The tradition says Angad gathered Nanak's bani and had it written down in Gurmukhi. That is the tradition's word — but it is certain that from Angad's time the written form of the bani began to take shape, and that it became, in Guru Arjan's time, the Guru Granth Sahib.

Pause and think — Angad did not give the letters a new form — he improved the old letters and taught them to all. Is improving something less than making it new? And how great a thing is it to have letters that can write your own speech?

7 · Khadur Sahib — Langar and Seva · · KHADUR SAHIB — LANGAR AND SEVA

After Nanak's death, Angad moved to Khadur Sahib — his wife Mata Khivi's village, in today's Tarn Taran district of Punjab. There he made the seat of his Guruship.

At Khadur there was everything that had been at Kartarpur — bani in the morning, work by day, kirtan in the evening, and langar. But the langar at Khadur had one special thing — it was run by Mata Khivi.

They say the food in Mata Khivi's langar never ran out. Whoever came, ate — and whoever came hungry, left with a full stomach. Mata Khivi herself served the food, and one saying of hers was famous in the sangat — in langar there is no great or small; whoever sits in the row is equal.

Angad himself worked in the langar too — washing vessels, kneading dough, fetching water. He said — service itself is true devotion. The one who works for others is closest to God.

At Khadur Angad began one more thing — the teaching of children. He taught children Gurmukhi, and with it he taught them bani too — so that the next generation would know both the letters and the bani.

Mata Khivi and the langar

The fame of Mata Khivi's langar is found in the Janamsakhis and Gurbilas — and the praise of Mata Khivi's langar is also in the Guru Granth Sahib itself, in the Vaar of Balwand and Satta, where it is said that in her langar there was no shortage of ghee and sugar. That praise is the strongest witness of Angad's own tradition.

Khadur — why?

Why Angad chose Khadur instead of Kartarpur as his seat, the tradition says Khadur was his wife's village and its sangat had called him there. History cannot say the reason with certainty — but Khadur became the seat of Angad's Guruship.

Pause and think — In Mata Khivi's langar there was no great or small. Around you, which place is it where all sit equal — and could you ever serve someone there?

8 · The Akhara — A Strong Body · · THE AKHARA — A STRONG BODY

At Khadur there was one more thing that became Angad's mark — the akhara. Outside the village, in an open place, there was a wrestling ground of earth — where wrestlers wrestled early in the morning.

Angad himself went to the akhara. He said — the one whose body is not strong cannot keep his mind strong either. Devotion does not mean only sitting and remembering the Name — devotion means the body is healthy too, and the mind too.

The young men of the sangat wrestled in the akhara, ran, and sweated in the dust. Then they bathed, ate in the langar, and read the bani. Angad said — the akhara in the morning, kirtan in the evening — the two are two sides of the same coin.

This thing grew very great in the Sikh tradition that followed — the teaching of miri-piri, of saint and soldier, whose foundation was laid in Angad's akhara.

The akhara — the tradition's story

The akhara at Khadur and Angad's emphasis on physical discipline are found in the Janamsakhis and Gurbilas. It is certain that Angad laid stress on physical strength — and in the time of the later Gurus, above all Guru Hargobind, this became the 'saint-soldier' tradition.

Pause and think — Angad said — without a strong body there is no strong mind. In your day, is there room for both play and study? And what makes you strong?

9 · The Question of Succession — Not to the Sons · · THE QUESTION OF SUCCESSION — NOT TO THE SONS

Nanak had given the seat not to his sons but to his disciple. Angad did the same — but the question before him was harder still. He had two sons — Datu and Dasu — and both felt the seat would surely pass from father to son.

But Angad said plainly — the seat belongs not to blood but to service. As Nanak had chosen me — seeing my service — so after me will come the one who stands foremost in service.

Datu did not like this. The tradition says Datu said to his father — you have given the seat to an outsider, so what becomes of us? Angad said — your work is to serve, not to ask for the seat.

It was the same thing Nanak had said at Kartarpur — and Angad repeated at Khadur. The seat is not the family's property; it is the responsibility of service.

Sri Chand and the Udasis

Nanak's elder son Sri Chand founded the Udasi order after the seat did not come to him — a sect of ascetics, which kept its own place in the Sikh tradition thereafter. The younger son, Lakhmi Das, stayed at Kartarpur and kept away from the question of the seat. This also appeared in the first book.

Datu's anger — the tradition's story

The story of Datu's anger and Angad's answer is found in the Janamsakhis. Datu's story continues further — after Amardas took the seat, Datu opposed him, and that will come in the next part.

Pause and think — Angad did not give the seat to his sons. Was that right? And around you — does responsibility always stay within the family, or does it also come by worth?

10 · The Guruship — 1539 to 1552 · · THE GURUSHIP — 1539 TO 1552

Angad's Guruship ran from 1539 to 1552 — thirteen years. Those thirteen years were quiet — no great journey, no great war. But in those very thirteen years the foundation of the Sikh sangat was made firm.

Every day Angad rose early, read the bani, taught children their letters, worked in the langar, and sang kirtan with the sangat in the evening. His life was like Nanak's life — with one difference. Nanak travelled; Angad sat in one place and built the sangat.

Angad also composed his own bani — 62 slokas, which stand today in the Guru Granth Sahib. His bani carries the same teaching as Nanak's bani — labour, the Name, and service — but in Angad's voice there is one more thing — humility.

In his slokas one thought returns again and again — the one who thinks himself small is closest to God. Angad kept himself small all his life — he said, I am only an ang of Nanak, his servant, not a Guru.

Angad's bani — 62 slokas

Guru Angad's 62 slokas are recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib — this is Angad's own bani, his firmest witness. In these slokas are humility, service, and the glory of the Name.

Thirteen quiet years

Very little is written in history about the years of Angad's Guruship — no great event, no war. Modern scholars (such as J. S. Grewal) say this very quiet was Angad's greatest gift — he gave Nanak's sangat a home, a script, and an everyday way of life.

Pause and think — For thirteen years Angad made no great journey — he sat in one place and built the sangat. Does great work always need a great journey — or can great work be done sitting in one place?

11 · Amardas's Service · · AMARDAS'S SERVICE

One day a man came to Khadur — Bhai Amardas. He lived near Goindwal, on the bank of the Beas river — a Vaishnav Hindu, who went to Haridwar every year and bathed in the Ganga.

The tradition says Amardas heard Bibi Amro — Angad's daughter — singing the bani one day. There was such sweetness in Amro's song that Amardas stopped. He asked — whose bani is this? Amro said — my father's, Guru Angad's — and his Guru's, Nanak's.

Amardas came to Khadur — and never left again. He became Angad's servant. For twelve years — about 1541 to 1552 — he served Angad.

His service became famous in the sangat. Every morning he rose, brought water from the Beas river, arranged Angad's bath, worked in the langar, and late at night sat beside Angad listening to the bani. They say that in twelve years not a single day passed on which Amardas fell short in service.

Angad watched — and said nothing. He knew the question of the seat was now being answered.

When did Amardas come to Khadur?

The year Amardas came to Khadur is taken in the sources as about 1541, and his twelve years of service as 1541–1552. This is the traditional reckoning — history cannot fix it to a certain date.

Bibi Amro's bani

Amardas coming to Khadur after hearing Bibi Amro's song is the Janamsakhis' story. Bibi Amro was Angad's daughter, and she was married into the family of Bhai Jassu of Goindwal — Amardas was connected to that same family.

Pause and think — For twelve years Amardas served every day — without tiring, without asking. Does service have a reward — or is service itself the reward?

12 · The Light Passes to Amardas · · THE LIGHT PASSES TO AMARDAS

In 1552 Angad's health began to fail. In the sangat the same question rose again — after Angad, who?

Angad called Amardas. He placed his hand on his head and said — Amardas, you have served for twelve years. Now this light is yours.

The sangat saw — the same thing happened that had happened in Nanak's time. The Guru changed, but the light stayed the same. One lamp lit another — the flame the same, the lamp new.

But this time one more thing happened. Angad's son Datu did not like it. The tradition says Datu kicked Amardas in anger — and Amardas bowed and said — brother, your foot is not hurt, is it? Datu went away in shame.

Amardas took up the seat — and Angad closed his eyes, calm, as one who sleeps after finishing his work.

Datu's kick — the tradition's story

The story of Datu kicking Amardas and Amardas's humble reply is found in the Janamsakhis. Its point is that Amardas's humility was itself his worth — and Datu's story does not end here; he kept opposing Amardas afterwards, and that will come in the next book.

Pause and think — Amardas was kicked — and he asked whether the foot of the one who kicked him was hurt. Is this what humility means — to worry for the other even when you are hurt?

13 · The Last Days — Khadur Sahib · · THE LAST DAYS — KHADUR SAHIB

Only a few days after passing on the light, on 29 March 1552, Guru Angad passed away at Khadur Sahib. He was forty-eight years old — a few days short of his forty-eighth birthday on 31 March.

The sangat bade him farewell as they had bade Nanak farewell — singing the bani, remembering the Name, and sharing the langar. At Khadur today there still stands Gurdwara Sri Angad Dev Sahib — the very place where Angad lived and where he died.

After Angad, Amardas took up the sangat — and the light that was in Nanak passed through Angad to Amardas, and today it is in the Guru Granth Sahib.

The date of death

According to the Sikh records, Guru Angad died on Chet vadi 4, Samvat 1609 — 29 March 1552 at Khadur Sahib. This is the date found in most sources, and it is the one used in this book.

Pause and think — Angad was forty-eight — he left younger than Nanak. But the foundation he laid in thirteen years — the script, the langar, the akhara, the sangat — still stands today. Is a person's gift measured by the years of his life?

To Think About · · TO THINK ABOUT

Angad's story is not the story of a king, not the story of a warrior. It is the story of a man who, even after becoming the Guru, still thought of himself as a disciple — Nanak's ang, Nanak's servant.

His greatest gift was no miracle — it was Gurmukhi. Giving the letters their form, teaching children, having the bani written down — that was the work by which Nanak's bani has reached us today. If Angad had not had the bani written down, perhaps we would not have Nanak's words at all.

Angad taught that devotion does not mean only sitting and remembering the Name — devotion means service, labour, and a strong body. Washing vessels in the langar, wrestling in the akhara, teaching children their letters — all of this is devotion too.

And the greatest thing — like Nanak, Angad did not let the seat become the family's property. He showed that a Guru is the one who serves — in whatever home he was born.

After Angad came seven more Gurus — Amar Das, Ram Das, Arjan, Hargobind, Har Rai, Har Krishan, Tegh Bahadur, and Gobind Singh. And in the end that light came to rest in the Guru Granth Sahib — which is the Guru of the Sikhs today. Their stories will come in the next books of this series.

But this second book ends here — at Khadur, one morning, with a quiet sangat. And with a question — if Angad were here today, which letter would he teach you first?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

The main source — Angad's own bani

The firmest foundation of this book is Guru Angad's own bani, recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib — 62 slokas. Where this book says 'Angad's own bani', this is its basis. Nanak's bani (974 shabads) was described in the first book.

The Janamsakhis and Gurbilas — the tradition's lives

The stories of Angad's life are found in the Janamsakhis (Puratan, Miharban, Bhai Bala) and in Gurbilas literature. They were written decades and centuries after the deaths of Nanak and Angad, and history and tradition are mixed in them. Every Janamsakhi story in this book is marked 'the tradition tells us' and explained in its own note.

The Vaars of Bhai Gurdas

In Bhai Gurdas's Vaar 1 there is the praise of Angad — he calls Angad the very form of Nanak, and praises his service and humility. It is the earliest poetic witness to Angad's life.

Mata Khivi's langar — the Granth's witness

The praise of Mata Khivi's langar is in the Guru Granth Sahib itself, in the Vaar of Balwand and Satta (Raag Ramkali), where it is said that in her langar there was no shortage of ghee and sugar. This is the strongest contemporary witness in this book.

Modern scholarship

The dates and events in this book were checked against the work of modern scholars — J. S. Grewal, 'A History of the Sikhs', Vol. 1; W. H. McLeod, 'Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion' and 'The Sikhs: History, Religion and Society'; Max Arthur Macauliffe, 'The Sikh Religion', Vol. 2; and the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala). Where the scholars and the Janamsakhis say different things, both are recorded in this book.

Gurmukhi — what the scholars say

What this book says about Gurmukhi agrees with modern scholarship — the letter forms already existed (from the Landa/Mahajani tradition), and Angad's role was to give them form, order them, and spread them. W. H. McLeod too called Angad the one who 'gave form' to Gurmukhi, not its inventor.

One clear thing

In this book Angad is not shown against any faith. He was a devotee of the Goddess, then became Nanak's disciple — and he never spoke ill of his earlier devotion. His message was not to divide, but to join.

The End · · THE END

The story is complete — but Angad's journey is not over yet.

In the next book — Guru Amar Das, who served for twelve years and then took up the seat — and who faced Datu's challenge.

Waheguru Ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji ki Fateh.
